lesson.title: y Equals a Constant: The Simplest Graph of a Line
lesson.summary: A horizontal line is the graph of every point sharing the same y-coordinate, described by the simple equation y equals a constant and always carrying zero slope.
lesson.body:
A horizontal line is one of the simplest graphs of a line you will ever plot, and it is the direct picture of zero slope. Because every point on a horizontal line shares the exact same y-coordinate, the equation describing it needs no x at all, it is simply y equals some constant number, often written y = c. No matter what x-value you choose, the y-value never changes, which is exactly why the graph never rises or falls as it runs left to right.

Consider the equation y equals 3. Some points that satisfy this equation are (negative 5, 3), (0, 3), and (4, 3). Notice the x-coordinates are all different, negative 5, 0, and 4, while every y-coordinate is 3. Plotting these points and connecting them produces a perfectly flat line running straight across the graph at height 3. Verify the slope using two of these points, say (negative 5, 3) and (4, 3): m equals (3 minus 3) divided by (4 minus negative 5), which is 0 divided by 9, equals 0. The slope of a horizontal line is always exactly 0, matching what you already learned about zero slope.

Slope-intercept form, y equals mx plus b, actually explains why the equation of a horizontal line drops the x-term entirely. Substituting m = 0 into that form gives y equals 0 times x plus b, and 0 times x is always 0, so the equation collapses to y equals b. The constant b is simply the shared y-coordinate, which is also the y-intercept of the line, since a horizontal line crosses the y-axis at exactly that height and nowhere else.

A horizontal line has no x-intercept unless the constant itself is 0, in which case the line is y equals 0, which is the x-axis itself. For any other constant, such as y equals 3, the line never touches the x-axis at all, because the y-coordinate is locked at 3 and can never become 0. This is different from a typical slanted line, which almost always crosses both axes somewhere.

Horizontal lines describe any real situation with a value that never changes over time, such as a speed limit sign posting 55 miles per hour regardless of location, or a fixed monthly rent that stays the same no matter how many months pass. Recognizing an equation of the form y equals a constant, with no x term present, should immediately tell you the graph is a flat horizontal line with zero slope, without needing to plot a single point.

Graphing a horizontal line is faster than graphing almost any other kind of line, precisely because its equation already tells you everything. To graph y equals 3, there is no need to compute a slope, find an x-intercept, or plot several points and hope they line up: draw a single straight line straight across the coordinate plane, passing through height 3 on the y-axis, and extend it in both directions. Every point along that line, no matter how far left or right, automatically satisfies the equation, since y is fixed at 3 while x is allowed to be anything at all. This is a useful case to master early, since it also serves as a clean check on your understanding of zero slope: if you ever compute a slope of 0 between two given points, you now know without any further work that the line connecting them must be horizontal, and its equation must be y equals whichever y-coordinate the two points shared.
